source.title: Towards a Robust Differentiable Architecture Search under Label Noise
source.authors: Christian Simon; Piotr Koniusz; Lars Petersson; Yan Han; Mehrtash Harandi

record.tranche_reason: Tests how label noise affects training and evaluation, and how clean versus noisy samples influence gradients over training; it does not use the original random-labeling setup.
record.gate_note: The study reports test accuracy under symmetric and asymmetric label noise and qualitative gradient-norm comparisons for clean versus noisy samples. It does not report results on completely random labels, training error for the noisy-label experiments, convergence time, or the regularizers named in V5. Cited results are not extracted.
record.test_reason: Figure 4 tests the test-error component of V4 in architectures obtained by NAS: test accuracy decreases as symmetric label noise increases from 0% to 20% to 50%. Perfect training-set fit is not established. The extracted gradient norms do not directly test V6's order of fitting.
record.authors_conclusion: The record accurately paraphrases the gradient analysis, but incompletely summarizes the paper's conclusion. The authors conclude that label noise harms vanilla DARTS and that nConv improves robustness and test accuracy with relatively small architectures. They interpret the gradient comparisons as evidence of reduced overfitting; those comparisons do not directly establish fitting order.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses DARTS and adds a learned noise-injecting convolution operator; it studies symmetric and asymmetric label corruption rather than random relabeling of the full training set.
record.method_sensitivity: Label-noise setting and use of nConv change the reported outcome: vanilla DARTS shifts from clean-sample to noisy-sample gradient dominance, while DARTS + nConv retains clean-sample dominance. The authors report that varying the noise mean did not affect performance significantly in the toy-data ablation.

fits_no_version.finding: Vanilla DARTS shifts from clean-sample gradient dominance early to noisy-sample dominance later; nConv maintains clean-sample dominance.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Clean and noisy samples exert different gradient influence over training, and adaptive noise injection changes that influence.

fits_no_version.finding: On the toy dataset with 20% corrupted labels, noise injection reduces hidden-representation mutual information with noisy labels and improves validation performance.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Adaptive noise injection can reduce representation dependence on corrupted labels and improve generalization.

record.peer_reviewed: IEEE Workshop/Winter Conference on Applications of Computer Vision
record.problems: The gradient comparisons are qualitative in the text and provide no numerical gradient norms. The reported gradient analysis uses CIFAR-10 with 50%-symmetric noise and does not directly measure which patterns are fitted or training error. Test-accuracy figure values are not recoverable with reliable model-condition assignments from the supplied flattened text.
record.rows_left_out: No result rows omitted. Test-accuracy results in Fig. 4 and other figures were not extracted because the supplied flattened figure text does not reliably associate numeric values with each model and condition.

untested.parts: Near-zero training error on completely random labels, chance test performance, and unchanged architecture and hyperparameters.
Relative time to fit true and random labels, and convergence slowing with increasing corruption.
Fitting shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, or Gaussian-noise inputs.
Perfect training-set fit at each corruption rate, behavior above 50% corruption through completely random labels, and direct evidence of simultaneously capturing signal and memorizing noise.
The necessity or sufficiency of weight decay, dropout, and data augmentation for random-label fitting and true-label generalization.
Direct comparison of when shared real-data patterns and noisy labels are fitted. Gradient norms and representation-label mutual information do not establish that order.

missing.what: V4 is tested outside the extracted rows. Figure 4 reports decreasing test accuracy across 0%, 20%, and 50% symmetric corruption for both methods on both CIFAR datasets. The record already declares these results omitted; they need rows to anchor the V4 verdict.

record.verdict_notes: No V6 verdict is warranted from gradient dominance alone. The V4 support concerns only the measured degradation in test performance over the tested corruption range.

versions.untested_parts: Completely random labels, chance test error, and unchanged architecture and hyperparameters.
Training time to fit true versus random labels and convergence as corruption increases.

Training-set fit or perfect training accuracy is not reported. The figures show test accuracy across label-noise rates, but precise values cannot be reliably assigned from the supplied flattened figure text.
Weight decay, dropout, and data augmentation as interventions on random-label fitting or true-label generalization.

The study tests clean versus noisy label samples under 50% symmetric label noise, not fully random labels; it measures gradient norms rather than directly measuring the order in which patterns are fitted.

rows.subject: Vanilla DARTS
rows.operation_detail: Compared gradient norms from clean-label and noisy-label samples during evaluation-phase training.
rows.measure: Relative gradient-norm contribution of clean-label versus noisy-label samples
rows.value: In the early epochs, samples with clean labels dominate over samples with noisy labels.
rows.note: The text describes the direction of the comparison; no numerical gradient norms are stated.
rows.check: Clean-sample gradient dominance measures training influence, not whether real patterns are fitted before noisy labels. The reported qualitative comparison is accurate.

rows.subject: Vanilla DARTS
rows.operation_detail: Compared gradient norms from clean-label and noisy-label samples during evaluation-phase training.
rows.measure: Relative gradient-norm contribution of clean-label versus noisy-label samples
rows.value: In the later epochs of the training, the reverse is true.
rows.note: The text says noisy-sample gradients dominate later, after clean-sample gradients dominate early.
rows.check: Later noisy-sample gradient dominance does not measure memorization timing. The original reversed state is also misleading: a later shift toward noise would be consistent with V6, rather than its opposite, if fitting had been measured.

rows.subject: DARTS + nConv
rows.operation_detail: Compared gradient norms from clean-label and noisy-label samples during evaluation-phase training.
rows.measure: Relative gradient-norm contribution of clean-label versus noisy-label samples
rows.value: The impact of the gradient of the clean samples dominates the impact of the gradient of the noisy samples throughout the entire training.
rows.note: The method includes the study's proposed nConv noise-injecting operator.
rows.check: Persistent clean-sample gradient dominance under the proposed mitigation does not establish whether or when noisy labels are fitted. It cannot justify a limits_scope verdict on V6.

relationships.condition: Vanilla DARTS and DARTS + nConv on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100, with 0%, 20%, and 50% symmetric label noise; test-error component only
relationships.reason: Figure 4 shows progressively lower test accuracy with increasing corruption for both methods and datasets. This verdict uses the text and figure omitted from the rows; it does not establish perfect training fit or the chance endpoint.
relationships.display_finding: Both methods showed progressively lower test accuracy on both datasets as corruption increased.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Vanilla DARTS on CIFAR-10 with 50%-symmetric label noise
reader_labels.reason: Clean-sample gradients dominate early, then noisy-sample gradients dominate later, consistent with different learning influence over training (R1, R2).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: DARTS + nConv on CIFAR-10 with 50%-symmetric label noise
reader_labels.reason: Clean-sample gradients dominate throughout training, so the temporal reversal described for vanilla DARTS does not hold with this operator (R3).
